messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Liam presents as a well-spoken 28-year-old social media manager, though his posture is tense and his gaze frequently drifts towards the window. He came to therapy at the urging of his girlfriend, four years after his honorable discharge from the Army. The event that haunts him occurred during his second tour in Afghanistan. He was in the passenger seat of a Humvee, part of a routine patrol on a dusty, sun-bleached road. He remembers the jarring lurch of the vehicle, a soundless flash of white light, and then a chaotic sequence of disconnected sensations: the metallic taste of blood, the high-pitched ringing in his ears, the sight of his sergeant’s grievously wounded leg. The memories don't form a coherent story; they exist as fragmented pieces that refuse to fit together. Sometimes, when he tries to recall the sequence of events, the whole memory feels so extreme and cinematic that he finds it hard to believe it actually happened to him.

In the months after returning home, Liam tried to slot back into his old life. He moved in with his girlfriend, landed a good job, and reconnected with friends. But the war had followed him home in ways he couldn't articulate. The sound of a news helicopter hovering over his downtown apartment building would send a jolt of ice through his veins, his heart hammering against his ribs as he fought the urge to seek cover. He began insisting on being the one to drive whenever he and his girlfriend went anywhere; the feeling of being a passenger, of not being in control of the vehicle's movement, was unbearable. Even a minor pothole could make him flinch. He was once on the subway and saw a man with a complex series of surgical scars on his arm, and Liam had to get off at the next stop, overwhelmed by a sudden, suffocating wave of dread. He couldn't explain to his girlfriend why; often, he experiences the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image attached, a phantom terror that descends without warning.

To manage this internal chaos, Liam’s world has gradually shrunk. He quit the gym he used to attend with his girlfriend, unable to tolerate the feeling of a racing heart and shortness of breath that a hard workout induced, as it felt too similar to the panic of the attack. At work, his role requires him to be agile and responsive, yet he finds himself spending hours rehearsing what he’s going to say before any client call, scripting his side of the conversation to avoid being caught off guard. He will cross the street to avoid walking past a police officer, the sight of the uniform a stark and unwelcome reminder. These strategies provide a temporary sense of safety but have deepened his isolation. He looks at his colleagues and friends and feels like he’s watching them from behind a thick wall of glass. He has come to believe he is permanently an outsider now, marked by an experience they could never comprehend.

Night offers no respite. Liam finds it nearly impossible to fall asleep, convinced on some primal level that he must remain alert for danger. He lies awake for hours, cataloging every creak of the floorboards, every distant siren. His girlfriend’s slightest movement in her sleep can make him jump. Last week, she came up behind him while he was working and gently placed a hand on his shoulder; he leapt from his chair with a strangled cry, his body reacting before his mind could identify the source of the touch. The fear in her eyes was the final catalyst for him seeking help. He carries a profound and private shame, a looping thought that somebody else, someone better trained or more aware, would not have gotten into this situation. He is terrified that he has been permanently changed for the worse, that the easygoing man he was before his deployment is gone for good, and that he will eventually drive away the last person who is trying to hold on to him.
